players.name: Jahmyr Gibbs
players.take: Gibbs has more touchdowns through three seasons than any other NFL player ever. At 24 years old, he’s entering his prime. And with fellow RB David Montgomery traded to Houston, he’s poised for a career-high workload. He is the consensus 1A to Bijan Robinson’s 1B this season, mostly because Jared Goff provides a more stable QB situation than Robinson has in Atlanta.

players.name: Bijan Robinson
players.take: Robinson led all players with 2,298 scrimmage yards last year. In addition to being one of the most elusive tackle breakers in the league, the fourth-year pro has quietly turned into one of the most prolific pass catching backs in the NFL, one of just two running backs (joining Christian McCaffrey) to earn 100-plus targets in 2025. There are question marks about the Falcons offense, but there’s little doubt that new Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski will feed Robinson both on the ground and in the passing game.

players.name: Ja’Marr Chase
players.take: The last time Joe Burrow played 17 games, Ja’Marr Chase put up the second-best fantasy season of any WR in the 2020s (behind Cooper Kupp in 2021) with 127 catches for 1,708 yards and 17 TDs. Don’t overthink it.

players.name: Puka Nacua
players.take: Nacua is one of the most talented and prolific pass catchers in the NFL, and in the Matthew Stafford–led Rams offense, the fourth-year pro has a strong chance to go back-to-back as fantasy’s top scoring receiver. But Nacua comes with some risk for fantasy drafters: He plays with a borderline reckless style, which makes him more of an injury gamble than most receivers. And he could face league discipline after checking into a rehab program and being named in a civil lawsuit over the offseason; the lawsuit states that Nacua made antisemitic remarks and forcibly bit a woman's shoulder.

players.name: Christian McCaffrey
players.take: In fantasy, McCaffrey is the living embodiment of the Talladega Nights adage “If you ain’t first, you’re last.” The 49ers’ do-it-all playmaker boasts multiple years of league-winning fantasy production … but has all too frequently been haunted by season-ruining injuries. The reality with CMC is that if he can stay healthy, he’s a fantasy cheat code who gives drafters what amounts to two players in one tidy roster spot. Last year, McCaffrey scored more fantasy points than any other skill player, ranking inside the top 12 among all players in both rushing fantasy points and receiving fantasy points.

players.name: Jaxon Smith-Njigba
players.take: Smith-Njigba broke out into fantasy superstardom in 2025, reeling in 119 passes for a league-high 1,793 yards and 10 touchdowns for the Super Bowl champion Seahawks and helping win fantasy managers plenty of their own titles along the way. While Seattle could look to spread the ball around more this year under new offensive play caller Brian Fleury, that doesn’t make JSN a bad or even necessarily a risky first-round pick: He still carries that elusive combination of a high floor and high ceiling for fantasy drafters.

players.name: Amon-Ra St. Brown
players.take: Amon-Ra has quietly become the most bankable player at the receiver position, logging 100-plus catches, 1,200 yards, and double-digit touchdowns in each of the past three seasons. The only other players who’ve done that three times in a row are Antonio Brown, Davante Adams, and Marvin Harrison Sr. ARSB is not a sexy first-round pick like some other players, but he might be the most reliable first-rounder.

players.name: Saquon Barkley
players.take: Barkley regressed in 2025, along with the rest of the Eagles offense. But maybe we're overthinking it now—he's still one of the most talented RBs in the NFL, if not in the history of the league. He'll get heavy volume on a run-first team, and if the Eagles add some more red-zone opportunities in 2026, Barkley could bounce back.

players.name: James Cook III
players.take: Cook led the league in rushing yards in 2025 and rushing touchdowns in 2024 yet still isn’t respected as an elite running back. Cook is basically the Amon-Ra St. Brown of running backs: boring but unlikely to let you down.

players.name: Jonathan Taylor
players.take: Taylor was well on his way to fantasy MVP status through the Colts’ first 10 games last year, a torrid stretch in which he notched four separate three-touchdown performances. Indy’s offense fell apart when Daniel Jones was lost for the season due to an Achilles injury, though, and Taylor’s numbers dipped down the stretch. But if Jones can get back to the field early on, the Colts running back could quickly regain the form we saw early on last year. Taylor should benefit from a quality run blocking offensive line and faces almost zero competition for touches.

players.name: Derrick Henry
players.take: When Lamar Jackson plays, Derrick Henry averages 17 fantasy points per game, a number only five other running backs have reached in each of the past two seasons. Father Time is getting tired, Henry isn't. Keep drafting him.

players.name: Ashton Jeanty
players.take: How much can we blame Jeanty for his mediocre rookie season? I think most of the fingers should point toward the terrible Raiders offensive line, below-average QB play, and checked-out coaching staff. Jeanty has the juice, and the Raiders signing one of the league’s best centers and hiring one of the best play callers should give him the ability to prove that. Jeanty was one of the best RBs in the NFL in yards after contact last season. He’s also 19th among all RBs in snaps inside the 10-yard line.

players.name: CeeDee Lamb
players.take: CeeDee suffered a high-ankle sprain in Week 3 and then got frame mogged by George Pickens, leading to just three touchdowns in 2025 and his least productive season since he was a rookie. A Lamb bounce back is baked into his cost, but he is the only top wide receiver on the board who’s at risk of statistically being the second-best receiver on his team.

players.name: Justin Jefferson
players.take: Entering last season, Justin Jefferson had scored more PPR fantasy points in his first five years than any other receiver in NFL history. But 2025 was a disaster, as quarterback J.J. McCarthy could not get Jefferson the ball. Kyler Murray is now the Vikings QB, and he will try to return Jefferson to his historic pace.

players.name: Chase Brown
players.take: When Joe Burrow plays, Chase Brown is an elite fantasy running back. He has finished as a top 5 RB in each of his past two seasons when playing alongside Burrow. He might not turn heads on draft night, but the 26-year-old, 2023 fifth-round pick is locked into a huge role in one of the league's most potent offenses.

players.name: Kenneth Walker III
players.take: The Chiefs gave Walker a big contract (three years, $43 million) and plan to feature him as their all-around back, capable of doing everything—blocking, catching passes, bruising between the tackles, and, most importantly, creating explosive run plays.

players.name: Omarion Hampton
players.take: The 2025 first-round pick is set to be the lead back on a Chargers team that upgraded tremendously at both offensive line and play caller this offseason. New OC Mike McDaniel could transform this offense into one of the best in the league, with Hampton leading the way on the ground. Hampton may share some of his workload with Keaton Mitchell or Kimani Vidal, but many backs could succeed in a McDaniel system.

players.name: A.J. Brown
players.take: "If you're not welcomed, not listened to, quietly withdraw. Don't make a scene,” A.J. Brown tweeted, thus loudly making a scene. Brown has a case as this year’s George Pickens: a talented diva whose effort waned but was then traded to a team with a better overall passer and offensive coordinator. But was Brown’s decline a physical one (he’s had knee issues for years), or was it just the result of a lack of effort?

players.name: De’Von Achane
players.take: Achane is elite, but the Dolphins are abysmal. While he might dominate the Dolphins passing game (Miami has the worst pass catching group the NFL's seen in years), he may need to collect his stats in garbage time this year. That’s a tall order for any running back.

players.name: Brock Bowers
players.take: Bowers is all systems go after a disappointing sophomore season hampered by a PCL strain. Bowers has arguably the least target competition in the league, should have improved QB play, and perhaps will have the biggest play calling upgrade as well. A reminder that this is the guy who finished third in the NFL in catches as a rookie. Everyone is asking which wide receiver is going to be the Jaxon Smith-Njigba of 2026. My money is on a certain tight end.

players.name: Nico Collins
players.take: Collins is a big-play alpha receiver who has posted three straight 1,000-yard seasons as the go-to guy in the Houston offense. There’s little doubt that he’s one of the most talented and explosive pass catchers in the NFL, but the Texans’ questionable offense—particularly quarterback C.J. Stroud’s inconsistent play—have kept Collins from reaching truly elite fantasy status. If Stroud can make a real jump in effectiveness in 2026, Collins could have top-five upside.

players.name: Drake London
players.take: London is a big, tough ball winner who dominates at the catch point and consistently commands targets. Over the past two seasons, he’s averaged 9.3 targets per game—fourth most among receivers—and without much competition for looks in the very shallow Atlanta receiving corps this year, he could once again hover near the league lead in target rate and post major fantasy production. The big fantasy hiccup with London, though, is the lack of clarity about who will be throwing him passes: Neither Tua Tagovailoa nor Michael Penix Jr. inspires much confidence.

players.name: Rashee Rice
players.take: Rashee Rice has been working his way back from a knee procedure that he couldn't rehab properly because he had to spend 30 days in jail for a parole violation (he tested positive for THC). On the field, Rice is one of the better fantasy assets in the league. Rice tore his LCL in 2024 and when he came back last season he was the WR5 in the eight games he played.

players.name: Trey McBride
players.take: Last year, McBride put together one of the most prolific seasons we’ve ever seen from a tight end, establishing a new Super Bowl–era record for catches at the position (126) while racking up 1,239 yards (the seventh-highest total among tight ends we’ve seen since 1966). The dynamic pass catcher certainly has the talent to repeat as the fantasy TE1 in 2026, but he could be due for some regression in his volume. The Cardinals likely won’t throw as many passes as they did last year (the team averaged a league-high 38.2 pass attempts per game), and even worse, if Arizona struggles early on, it’s possible that quarterback Jacoby Brissett could cede starts to third-round rookie Carson Beck, which would almost surely hurt the team’s efficiency on offense.

players.name: George Pickens
players.take: Pickens delivered a perception-altering performance last year by shattering his career highs in basically every counting stat. He is in a contract year (again) and figures to remain an elite red zone option on an elite offense.

players.name: Chris Olave
players.take: Olave put concussion fears to rest last year by playing in 16 games for the Saints and racking up 100 catches for 1,163 yards and nine touchdowns to finish as a top-12 fantasy receiver in all three formats (standard, half-PPR, PPR). Freshly signed to a big offseason extension, the fifth-year pro looks poised for another huge season in 2026. He’ll face a little competition for targets from the newly drafted rookie Jordyn Tyson, but in the Saints’ pass-happy, up-tempo offense under play caller Kellen Moore and ascending quarterback Tyler Shough (New Orleans ranked sixth in pass attempts and 11th in plays per game last year), Olave should see more than enough opportunities to push for a top-10 finish once again.

players.name: Emeka Egbuka
players.take: Egbuka’s rookie season was a tale of two extremes. Through the first five weeks last year, it looked like he was on his way to being one of the best fantasy picks of the season, racking up 445 yards and five touchdowns in that early stretch. But after he suffered a hamstring strain in Week 6, Egbuka’s production fell off a cliff. Presumably fully healthy again and with Mike Evans gone to San Francisco, Egbuka looks positioned to take up the mantle as the team’s go-to guy. He’s a prime bounce-back candidate.

players.name: Malik Nabers
players.take: Nabers tore his ACL last September, and the injury required a cleanup procedure this spring. It is still unclear when he will be 100 percent healthy. Nabers is a borderline first-round pick at full strength, but he’s an injury gamble right now. Monitor his status.

players.name: DeVonta Smith
players.take: DeVonta will dominate Philadelphia’s passing game now that A.J. Brown is gone. Smith, the former Heisman winner, has had borderline elite efficiency in limited snaps without Brown. Smith’s success depends on how well Jalen Hurts adapts to a new scheme under Sean Mannion, Hurts’s 11th offensive coordinator in as many years.

players.name: Josh Allen
players.take: Allen is probably the best fantasy quarterback ever. He has finished as the no. 1 or no. 2 fantasy quarterback in six straight years. Rushing yards are worth 2.5 times more than passing yards, and Allen runs the most in December, when the fantasy playoffs are on the line. The only issue with taking Allen is that the fantasy QB position is deep this year.

players.name: Ladd McConkey
players.take: McConkey’s disappointing sophomore year should be a thing of the past with Mike McDaniel calling plays and Keenan Allen no longer challenging him for targets. McConkey will be the focal point in what could be an elite Los Angeles offense.

players.name: Tetairoa McMillan
players.take: McMillan lived up to his predraft hype with a strong rookie campaign for the Panthers last year, reeling in 70 catches for 1,014 yards and seven touchdowns. He wasted no time establishing himself as the team’s no. 1 receiver, and with very little competition for targets (Jalen Coker is likely the team’s no. 2 wideout), he’s got a good shot at surpassing those numbers this year. McMillan’s ceiling could be stifled if Bryce Young fails to take another step forward, but the big playmaking receiver should have a solid floor.

players.name: Tee Higgins
players.take: In games Joe Burrow has started, Tee Higgins has scored 12.9 fantasy points per game over the past three seasons. Higgins tends to miss a few games each year due to injury (he hasn’t played a full season since 2022), but when he’s on the field he provides a safe floor (WR11 last year) and a very high ceiling (WR4 in 2024).

players.name: Kyren Williams
players.take: Williams has something as valuable as almost anything else in fantasy football: the implicit, unshakable trust of one Sean McVay. That trust has translated into major volume and lots of fantasy points over the past three years, and it's sure to do the same in 2026. The only problem for Williams, and it’s the reason he’s not ranked even higher, is that McVay seems to trust Blake Corum a lot now, too. Corum ate into Williams’s previously dominant snap and carry share in the second half of last year, and we could see L.A. leaning even more into the committee approach this year.

players.name: Josh Jacobs
players.take: Jacobs was arrested on multiple charges related to domestic violence over the offseason, but any subsequent suspensions are likely to come in 2027. He figures to continue to be a three-down back for the Packers this year after a disappointing season in which he didn’t top 100 yards once.

players.name: Jaylen Waddle
players.take: Waddle has run 519 routes with Tyreek Hill off the field since 2022—and he has the third-best yards per route run among all WRs over that stretch. This offseason, the Broncos traded a first-round pick for Waddle, who now steps into one of the pass-happiest offenses in the league with ascending QB Bo Nix and proven play caller Sean Payton. Waddle has proved his abilities in Miami, and will now get a chance to be the guy for the first time in his career.

players.name: Jeremiyah Love
players.take: The Cardinals selected Love with the third pick in this year’s draft because he possesses rare big-play ability both on the ground and in the pass game. And like almost every running back who is picked as high as he was, he’s very likely to be a major factor in his offense from day one—providing a solid floor for fantasy drafters. But there are reasons to believe that he could fail to live up to the hype: For starters, the Cardinals will likely be trailing in a lot of games this year as they take on one of the toughest schedules in the NFL—and that could limit Love’s opportunities. And the rookie’s also got stiff competition for passing game and goal-line work from wily veterans James Conner and Tyler Allgeier.

players.name: Javonte Williams
players.take: Williams will likely dominate the backfield again in 2026 for one of the NFL’s best offenses. He had an unexpected revival as the Cowboys’ lead back last year after his promising career in Denver was derailed by a knee injury. Williams is one of the NFL’s least efficient running backs in the passing game, but he’s still a three-down back on an elite offense.

players.name: Lamar Jackson
players.take: Lamar had the least Lamar-like season of his career in 2025, posting career lows in multiple categories including fantasy points per game, rushing yards per game, and sack percentage. In my view, most of this can be chalked up to a nasty hamstring injury in Week 4 that lingered throughout the season. Before the injury Lamar was the QB1, averaging over 27 fantasy points per game from Weeks 1-3, which would have been the second-highest average of his career. New play caller Declan Doyle should provide a fresh new coat of paint on an offense that started to peel in places last year.

players.name: Drake Maye
players.take: Maye was the no. 2 QB in fantasy last year and nearly won MVP after becoming the NFL’s best deep passer and leading the league with a 72.0 completion percentage, an unusual combo. Even with a (much) harder schedule, Maye will likely still have elite rushing ability (450 yards last year), and the replacement of Stefon Diggs with A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs should offset some of the natural regression Maye was due to have.

players.name: Mike Evans
players.take: Evans needs to prove that he can stay healthy—and that could be a big ask for this seemingly cursed 49ers team—but he has a chance to smash expectations in 2026 as the focal point of the San Francisco passing attack. Ricky Pearsall is out for the year with a PCL injury, and George Kittle may miss a month or more as he works to get back from a torn Achilles tendon, leaving Evans as the primary target in what’s typically been a highly efficient and high-scoring offense.

players.name: Colston Loveland
players.take: Loveland was the no. 2 tight end for the second half of last season and is widely considered a main piece of the Bears’ passing attack this year at just 22 years old. He’s a trendy sleeper who could go high.

players.name: Terry McLaurin
players.take: McLaurin and Jayden Daniels have a mind-meld connection, as evidenced by McLaurin scoring a franchise-record 13 touchdowns in 2024. Now recovered from his 2025 quad injury, McLaurin has a firm grip on the no. 1 receiver job even with Stefon Diggs in town, and he should be the focal point of the passing offense under new coordinator David Blough.

players.name: DJ Moore
players.take: Moore will likely dominate the Bills’ passing game but is undervalued because fantasy GMs are kind of tired of him. But Bills head coach Joe Brady went out of his way to reunite with Moore, who played for him in Carolina, and Moore will likely be the Temu Stefon Diggs of the Buffalo offense as the clear no. 1 amid many role players. He’s a clear bounce-back candidate.

players.name: Tyler Warren
players.take: Warren could benefit this year not only from Daniel Jones’s return from an Achilles tear but also from the shake-up in the Colts’ passing game hierarchy. With Michael Pittman off to Pittsburgh in an offseason trade, the second-year tight end looks set to gobble up a greater percentage of the team’s short and intermediate targets. After ranking fifth among all tight ends in targets per game last year (6.6), Warren has a shot at leading the position in that metric this season.

players.name: Zay Flowers
players.take: The soon-to-be 26-year-old receiver enters his fourth season in the NFL with a big, fat new contract and a new play caller, Declan Doyle, who seems keen on getting Zay the ball as much as possible. Flowers always has been extremely productive in between the 20-yard lines—it’s the red zone that’s the problem. In his past two seasons he is 50th in red zone targets among wide receivers. If Zay could double his previous high in touchdowns (five), he would be one of best mid-round selections in fantasy this season.

players.name: Breece Hall
players.take: If Hall played for any team other than the Jets, he might be a fantasy darling. But because he is on the Jets, the focus is on the doubts instead of Hall’s great offensive line, big contract extension, and three-down skill set. Hall is working for a potential lame duck head coach (Aaron Glenn), an offensive coordinator who has been out of the NFL for two years (Frank Reich), and a quarterback the Jets ditched more than a decade ago (Geno Smith). If you believe in the Jets, take Breece Hall.

players.name: Cam Skattebo
players.take: Skattebo is more myth than man. He ran into telephone poles as a child and still plays like it. Skattebo was a revelation in fantasy last year, briefly looking like a league winner as a crucial Giants pass catcher and goal-line back before breaking his leg and dislocating his ankle. Skattebo says he is fully healed, and if he is trusted again on third downs and at the goal line, he will be valuable in fantasy. But it all depends on the Tasmanian Devil’s health.

players.name: Jayden Daniels
players.take: Daniels looked like RGIV after a rookie season that revived football in Washington but then had an injury-plagued second season. Daniels’s deadeye deep ball, mind-meld with Terry McLaurin, new complement (Stefon Diggs), and elite scrambling ability make him a diamond in fantasy. The only question is whether string-bean Jayden—who dislocated his elbow last season—can stay on the field.

players.name: Luther Burden III
players.take: Burden is perhaps the most-hyped player of the offseason. Head coach Ben Johnson can’t stop raving about the second-year wideout and the power-slot role he could fill (like a more athletic Amon-Ra St. Brown) for the Chicago offense. The downside is that Burden injured his groin in training camp and may not be ready for Week 1. And when he does come back, his playing time might be limited, as Chicago has many mouths to feed.

players.name: Davante Adams
players.take: At 33 years old, Adams doesn’t move quite like he used to, and he’s more of an injury risk than ever. But the man can clearly still route up opposing defensive backs, especially in one-on-one situations near the goal line, where space gets tighter. Adams was the Rams’ de facto goal-line back last year, but he just did his work on the outside, racking up a league-best 14 touchdown catches on 27 end zone targets. Those numbers are likely to regress a bit in 2026, but not necessarily by a lot.

players.name: Garrett Wilson
players.take: Wilson is talented but has been hampered by being a Jet, and 2026 is no different. He is working with a quarterback whom the Jets gave up on more than a decade ago (Geno Smith), an offensive coordinator who has been out of the NFL for two years (Frank Reich), and a coach who will likely get fired at the end of the year (Aaron Glenn). Perhaps Wilson can succeed amid all that dysfunction, but it is hard to bank on.

players.name: Christian Watson
players.take: Watson tore his ACL in January 2025 but recovered remarkably quickly and instantly imbued the Packers offense with explosiveness down the stretch last season. Green Bay let Romeo Doubs leave in free agency and traded Dontayvion Wicks, which suggests that Watson will be the focal point of the passing game (and that Matthew Golden will have an increased role as well).

players.name: D’Andre Swift
players.take: Swift finished as the RB16 last year in what was perhaps his best season as a pro. He's a solid RB2 in a promising offense, but there are plenty of mouths to feed in Chicago that keep his ceiling a little lower than some of the other top fantasy backs.

players.name: David Montgomery
players.take: Montgomery has a proven track record as a do-it-all, high-volume back, and the Texans signed him to not only carry a heavy load for the team in 2026 but also hopefully revive what’s been one of the worst run games in the league over the past few seasons. Monty is still a big-time tackle breaker, and he has soft hands in the pass game, so he has a solid floor as an RB2. But we’ll need to see a big improvement from the team’s line (which includes new additions in free agents Wyatt Teller and Braden Smith and rookie first-rounder Keylan Rutledge) for him to significantly outperform his ADP.

players.name: Rome Odunze
players.take: Odunze has been the least efficient WR in the NFL since he was drafted in 2024, per yards per target over expectation. There are excuses—coaching in 2024, foot injuries in 2025—but there’s a clear fear that he will become third in the Bears’ pecking order behind both wide receiver Luther Burden III and tight end Colston Loveland.

players.name: Travis Etienne Jr.
players.take: The four-year, $48 million contract that the Saints gave to Etienne over the offseason would seem to imply that he’ll hold the team’s lead back role. But it was a lot easier to get excited about Etienne’s fantasy ceiling before Alvin Kamara unexpectedly returned to the team on a renegotiated one-year, $6 million deal last month. Kamara is likely to eat into Etienne’s opportunities for high-value touches in the form of passing game and goal-line work and could ultimately drag down his fantasy upside.

players.name: Joe Burrow
players.take: There’s more riding on this season in Cincinnati than people might think. Burrow hasn’t made the playoffs since 2022, and the Bengals haven’t finished better than third in the division over that stretch. Burrow has played a full season just once since 2022 and needs to string together a healthy campaign to keep any hopes of a Super Bowl alive in Cincinnati. We know what Burrow is capable of—he was the QB3 in 2024—he just needs to stay healthy.

players.name: Jameson Williams
players.take: Detroit’s old offensive coordinator John Morton lost play calling duties in part because he couldn’t get Williams the ball. Dan Campbell’s new OC, Drew Petzing, likely won’t have the same problem. Williams is a boom-or-bust burner who averaged 85 yards per game in the second half of last season. Tight end Sam LaPorta was hurt for that stretch, but Williams has earned an increased role even with LaPorta healthy.

players.name: Jalen Hurts
players.take: Hurts is on his 11th offensive coordinator in 11 years. Until last season, Hurts had one of the highest weekly floors and highest weekly ceilings ever for a fantasy quarterback. The Eagles offense, especially the offensive line, looked mortal in 2025, but a return to form could make Hurts a league-winning player.

players.name: Justin Herbert
players.take: Herbert lost both of his star tackles for the majority of last season. In the four games in which Herbert had just one of his tackles healthy, he averaged 0.44 EPA/dropback, which would have led every QB over any of the past five seasons. He averaged 21.6 FPG over that stretch, which would have made him the QB1. A healthy offensive line alone should give him a huge boost, and the addition of Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator is one of the biggest play calling upgrades in the league.

players.name: Quinshon Judkins
players.take: Judkins’s promising rookie season ended abruptly, after he broke his leg in Week 16. Eight months later he is back and seemingly healthy at training camp. The track record of players coming off of broken fibulas isn't great (see Tony Pollard in 2023), and the Browns offense projects to be one of the worst in the league this season, making Judkins a risky bet in the middle rounds.

players.name: Bucky Irving
players.take: As a healthy rookie, Irving was one of the most dynamic running backs in the NFL, racking up 1,514 scrimmage yards and eight scores to become one of the surprise breakouts at the position. In his second season last year, his elusiveness and efficiency cratered, mainly due to debilitating shoulder and foot injuries that limited him to just 865 scrimmage yards and four TDs in 10 games. The optimist in us would like to believe that as long as he’s healthy, he’ll go back to doing what he did as a rookie. But with the newly signed Kenneth Gainwell likely to steal passing game touches and Sean Tucker taking goal-line looks, Irving’s volume could be limited.

players.name: Rhamondre Stevenson
players.take: Despite all the hype around rookie running back TreVeyon Henderson, Stevenson maintained the lead role last year. Once again, Henderson is being drafted ahead of Stevenson, but once again, Stevenson might be the better back in fantasy. Stevenson is less explosive, but his blocking is stronger and earns him snaps on passing downs. He has superior vision as a ballcarrier, too. So Stevenson may be the smarter, if much less sexy, fantasy pick.

players.name: Jadarian Price
players.take: Price should get a crack at lead-back duties as Seattle’s first-rounder, and he could far outplay his ADP if he gets big volume or receives more work than expected in the passing game. Ultimately, though, there’s a risk that Price will fall into a dreaded running back time-share and sub out on third downs and near the goal line. With George Holani factoring in and Zach Charbonnet due back at some point this season after an ACL tear, Price may disappoint in fantasy as a rookie.

players.name: Caleb Williams
players.take: Williams set the Chicago record for passing yards last year and might become the first 4,000-yard passer in Bears history this year. He is surrounded by young and talented playmakers and has a bad defense that might force the Bears into high-scoring matchups. Add in Williams’s rushing potential, and he has top-five upside.

players.name: TreVeyon Henderson
players.take: Henderson is an explosive play waiting to happen, but he lost a lot of playing time to veteran Rhamondre Stevenson last season because of his limitations as a blocker and imperfect rushing vision. Henderson will be drafted high because of his explosiveness, but he is unlikely to completely take the backfield from Stevenson.

players.name: Trevor Lawrence
players.take: A few things people might not know about Trevor Lawrence: Last year, he had the single best fantasy playoff run by a QB in NFL history (32.86 PPG). He’s tied for third among all QBs in rushing TDs since 2022.

players.name: Parker Washington
players.take: Washington was one of the biggest surprises of the last fantasy season, clocking in as the WR11 over the final eight games. Now he’s been getting constant praise from head coach Liam Coen in training camp. Parker is surrounded by former first-round picks (Travis Hunter, Brian Thomas Jr.) and proven vets (Jakobi Meyers) but might have earned himself the role of WR1 in Jacksonville.

players.name: Brian Thomas Jr.
players.take: Thomas is a former first-round pick entering his third year who was the overall WR4 as a rookie in an offense that finished as the second-highest-scoring offense in the final five weeks of the season. Not a bad bet at his ADP!

players.name: Sam LaPorta
players.take: LaPorta had one of the best rookie seasons ever for a tight end, with 10 touchdowns in 2023, but he mildly disappointed in 2024 and then missed half of 2025 with a back injury. Now, LaPorta is an industry favorite to return to top-five tight end status, and he could have major upside in a talented Lions offense.

players.name: Bhayshul Tuten
players.take: Tuten could be the next man up in Liam Coen’s running back–friendly system, which saw Bucky Irving finish his rookie season as the RB7 in 2024 and Travis Etienne become the RB13 in 2025. The only thing standing in his way is newly signed Chris Rodriguez, whom Coen coached while at Kentucky. Tuten is a gamble, but one with high upside.

players.name: Marvin Harrison Jr.
players.take: As a former fourth pick, Harrison has been a massive disappointment relative to the expectations set for him, but don’t rule out a breakout in 2026. Playing in a new offense under head coach and play caller Mike LaFleur could provide a big boost, and the continuity that Jacoby Brissett brings as the team’s returning starter at quarterback can’t hurt, either.

players.name: Kyle Pitts
players.take: Are you prepared to get hurt again? Pitts has been a perennial fantasy disappointment in Atlanta, and while new head coach Kevin Stefanski loves his tight ends, an offense quarterbacked by either Tua Tagovailoa or Michael Penix Jr. doesn't inspire much confidence. Plus, Drake London is the clear top target on this team, and Bijan Robinson will get plenty of touches as well.

players.name: Tony Pollard
players.take: Things can’t really get worse for the Titans offense, which finished 31st in yards and 30th in points scored last season. Pollard still saw more than 16 touches per game last year, which was 20th in the league, ahead of guys like Kenneth Walker III and D’Andre Swift. Pollard will likely be the lead back once again on a team that can only improve.

players.name: Jaylen Warren
players.take: Warren is entering his fifth year on the Steelers as a productive and dependable piece of the offense. He finished as the RB19 last year in points per game and is coming off a career-high 1,291 yards and eight TDs from scrimmage. Unfortunately, he often shares the backfield with someone else. This year it’s Rico Dowdle, who will likely hoover up the majority of the early-down work in the run game.

players.name: Michael Wilson
players.take: Wilson is a riddle, wrapped in a mystery, inside an enigma. When Marvin Harrison was out with injuries last year, Wilson turned into one of the highest-scoring receivers in the game. But when Harrison was on the field, Wilson was unplayable in fantasy. The fact that the Cardinals have a new coach and play caller in Mike LaFleur only makes things more difficult to predict. If LaFleur changes up the way he uses his receivers, allowing both Harrison and Wilson to move around the formation and play in different spots, both players could produce big fantasy numbers. But right now, it’s impossible to guess just how the target split will shake out.

players.name: Quentin Johnston
players.take: After a disappointing rookie year, the former first-round pick quietly pieced together productive back-to-back seasons in L.A., and the Chargers picked up his fifth-year option. New offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel has compared parts of Johnston’s game to Julio Jones’s and Andre Johnson’s this offseason. Johnston had more touchdowns in each of his last two years (eight) than Ladd McConkey has ever had in a season. He is one of our favorite late-round selections.

players.name: Dak Prescott
players.take: After Joe Burrow, Prescott is the premier pocket-passing QB in fantasy football. Dallas’s cup runneth over on offense, with playmakers CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens and a young offensive line containing three guys named Tyler. Prescott led the league in completions two of the past three years, but if the Cowboys defense becomes average, reducing the need to pass the ball, his fantasy value could decline.

players.name: Tucker Kraft
players.take: Kraft was dominating the tight end position with six touchdowns in eight weeks last year until he tore his ACL. Kraft admittedly was running hot on touchdowns rather than massive target share or volume, which might be unsustainable, and his injury recovery might hamper his explosiveness. The boring (but sound) advice is to avoid this kind of profile, but that ignores that Kraft might just be awesome.

players.name: Carnell Tate
players.take: Breakout wide receivers usually follow a three-part checklist: heavy volume + good QB + good play caller. New OC Brian Daboll is partly responsible for the ascension of Josh Allen and the resurrection of Daniel Jones, and now former no. 1 pick Cam Ward is his next assignment. If Ward makes the leap, Carnell Tate will benefit.

players.name: Jonathon Brooks
players.take: In just his third game as a pro back in 2024, Brooks re-tore his previously reconstructed ACL, an injury that forced him to miss the rest of his rookie campaign and all of the 2025 season as well. Now, finally, the former second-rounder is fully healthy and reportedly looking spry at training camp—and he’s got a shot at taking over for Rico Dowdle as a complement to Chuba Hubbard in the Panthers backfield. He might even have a shot at taking over lead-back duties, too.

players.name: DK Metcalf
players.take: Metcalf ended his first season on the Steelers with a career low in receiving yards (850) and his lowest catch total (59) since his rookie season. Even in a Mike McCarthy–led offense, it’s hard to see huge upside for Metcalf, especially after the addition of Michael Pittman and second-round rookie Germie Bernard. Metcalf has not scored double-digit touchdowns since 2021.

players.name: Rico Dowdle
players.take: Dowdle has had the career of a late bloomer, doing little in his first four seasons in the league before posting back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons in Dallas and Carolina the past two years. Now in Pittsburgh and reunited with Mike McCarthy, Dowdle projects to be the thunder to Jaylen Warren’s lightning and should see significant early-down work. His lack of production in the passing game caps his upside, but Dowdle could provide flex appeal as a productive runner behind an up-and-coming offensive line.

players.name: Harold Fannin Jr.
players.take: Fannin set the single-season catch and yards record for a tight end in college football and followed it up by setting the single-season catch record for a Browns rookie. He has a little bit more competition now in rookies KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston, but new HC Todd Monken has a history of using his talented tight ends, and Fannin definitely qualifies. The QB play is another story.

players.name: Brock Purdy
players.take: The perpetually underrated Purdy looks like he'll have value again this year. He’s finished as a top-10 fantasy quarterback (in points per game) in each of the past three seasons and has a great shot at doing the same in 2026. Purdy needs to stay healthy this year. But he’s proved to be one of the most efficient passers in the game, and he’s not afraid to use his wheels to pick up first downs and add rushing points to his fantasy bottom line.

players.name: Bo Nix
players.take: Nix enters his third year under head coach Sean Payton fresh off a QB10 finish that saw him lead the NFL in pass attempts. And after the team traded a first-round pick for wide receiver Jaylen Waddle, it's possible that Denver will pass even more. From an efficiency standpoint, Nix was up and down last year, but the pass-happy scheme and his willingness to use his legs (356 rushing yards and five TDs) make him a solid selection for those following a late-round QB draft strategy.

players.name: Chuba Hubbard
players.take: It’s a plus for Hubbard that Rico Dowdle left for Pittsburgh in free agency, and he’s the favorite to play the lead-back role for the Panthers in 2026. But with Jonathon Brooks seemingly healthy and finally ready to get back on the field, Hubbard’s grasp on that job is a tenuous one. It also doesn’t help that both of the team’s starting tackles are likely to miss the start of the regular season, with Ickey Ekwonu working back from a torn patellar tendon and Taylor Moton dealing with blood clots.

players.name: Jayden Reed
players.take: Reed is talented, plays bigger than his size, and is always getting designed touches around the goal line. Reed had a bad 2025, undergoing foot surgery and breaking his collarbone, but he should be healthy to start this season. He has played almost exclusively in three-receiver sets but could be much more valuable if he rotates in with Matthew Golden in two-receiver sets this year.

players.name: Josh Downs
players.take: Downs is an impressive route runner with reliable hands, but he doesn’t get onto the field enough. He has primarily operated when the Colts have three receivers on the field (11 personnel) but heads to the sideline when they play in two-receiver sets—thus limiting his ability to rack up enough targets and catches to contribute consistently in fantasy. If that changes this year—and there are indications that it will now that Michael Pittman has gone to Pittsburgh—Downs has a chance to break out.

players.name: Courtland Sutton
players.take: Sutton showed some chemistry with Bo Nix last season, notching 74 receptions for 1,017 yards and seven touchdowns. But his upside is significantly capped after the team added Jaylen Waddle in the offseason. Other young receivers like Pat Bryant and Troy Franklin may also start to cut into Sutton’s production.

players.name: Jaxson Dart
players.take: Dart ran for nine touchdowns and had five concussion checks in the blue tent last year, as his brashness made him beloved but also brittle. With John Harbaugh now running the show in New York, Dart will probably play more but run (a little) less, though he could remain a top-12 QB thanks to his rushing ability.

players.name: Kyler Murray
players.take: Kyler could be the single best value pick of any QB in fantasy football. He was cut from Arizona and is now starting for the Vikings to clean up the mess J.J. McCarthy made last year. Kyler does not play exactly like Sam Darnold or Kirk Cousins, but he’s probably talented enough to reinvigorate the Vikings and could even rush for 572 yards, as he did in 2024. There’s a risk that his style won’t work for Kevin O’Connell, but the upside is immense.

players.name: Jordan Addison
players.take: Addison’s just 24 and will likely be a strong value this season if Kyler Murray revives the Vikings offense after the J.J. McCarthy disaster. Addison has scored a lot of touchdowns by beating one-on-one coverage in the end zone while defenses pay attention to Justin Jefferson, similar to what Calvin Ridley did in Atlanta opposite Julio Jones.

players.name: Wan’Dale Robinson
players.take: Receivers who had the fifth-most targets in the NFL over the past two seasons—and who just got four-year, $70 million contracts—don't often fall outside the top 100 in fantasy drafts. Despite the targets, Wan’Dale was the WR21 and WR55 over the past two seasons, and he has yet to catch more than four TDs in a season. Now he’s in Tennessee under Brian Daboll, and you could probably do worse than taking him in roughly the 11th round of your draft.

players.name: Blake Corum
players.take: For the first time in years, the Rams’ backfield could be a time-share. From Week 7 on last season, Corum got 39 percent of the team’s rushing carries and, critically, saw 44 percent of the team’s totes inside the 5-yard line. With a healthy Kyren Williams on the field, Corum is a flex play option. But if Williams misses any time, Corum could be one of the best handcuff running backs in fantasy.

players.name: RJ Harvey
players.take: Harvey was a rookie fantasy darling who didn't quite end up panning out last year, finishing as the RB27. Sean Payton offenses can be hard to predict, and Harvey had less playing time than expected last year. With the return of JK Dobbins and the addition of RB Jonah Coleman via the draft, Harvey will likely be part of a committee again this season. Scoring 12 touchdowns kept him relevant in fantasy last season. Can he do that again?

players.name: Michael Pittman Jr.
players.take: Pittman joins the Steelers after six productive seasons in Indianapolis. He is a tough, big-bodied wide receiver who should act as the security blanket over the middle of the field for Aaron Rodgers. In Weeks 1-10 last year, Pittman was the WR10. His talent might be slightly underrated at this point, but the Steelers’ limited offense and crowded pass catching unit cap his upside.

players.name: Mark Andrews
players.take: For the first time since 2021, Andrews will not be playing alongside Isaiah Likely. That season, Andrews had a career-high 107 catches, more than 1,300 yards, and nine TDs. Granted, he was 26 that year, and now he’s about to turn 31, but there is room for Andrews to become a TD hog again in this Baltimore offense.

players.name: J.K. Dobbins
players.take: When Dobbins plays, he delivers. The problem is that he never plays. He played 10 games last year, 13 in 2024, one in 2023, and eight in 2022. The Broncos just drafted another running back, Jonah Coleman, in the fourth round, diluting this backfield even more.

players.name: Alec Pierce
players.take: The Colts gave Pierce a massive four-year, $114 million contract over the offseason after the speedy pass catcher notched a 47-catch, 1,003-yard, six-touchdown season in 2025, and that deal could point to a big boost in Pierce’s target rate and overall fantasy value going forward. But the fifth-year pro is still working to get back on the field after having offseason ankle surgery, and there’s really no guarantee that even when he does return, Indianapolis will look to make him a bigger focal point in the offense.

players.name: Travis Kelce
players.take: About to turn 37, Kelce enters his 14th season on the Chiefs. Surprisingly, he was the TE6 last year before Patrick Mahomes tore his ACL in Week 15. The Chiefs made practically no changes to their receiving unit this offseason, making Kelce a somewhat under-the-radar selection in the later rounds.

players.name: Jordan Mason
players.take: Perhaps the cheapest starting running back in fantasy, Mason is likely to lead the Vikings in touches this season. Minnesota could easily double its nine carries inside the 5-yard line last year. The only issue is that pass catching work will go to Aaron Jones and Zavier Scott.

players.name: Chris Godwin Jr.
players.take: After suffering a dislocated ankle midway through the 2024 season, Godwin struggled to get back to form in 2025. He missed the first three weeks of the season, briefly returned in Weeks 4 and 5, and then missed another six games as he worked to get back to full health. Ultimately, he played nine games last year and never really looked quite like himself, finishing with 33 catches for 360 yards and two touchdowns. Godwin’s now 30 years old, but he’s presumably fully past the ankle injury that limited him so dramatically last year. With Mike Evans gone, Godwin may find himself as one of the focal points of Tampa Bay’s passing game once again.

players.name: Jakobi Meyers
players.take: Meyers came to Jacksonville midseason in 2025 via trade and made an immediate impact, providing stability to a chaotic receiving corps. This season, Meyers has much more competition, with the emergence of Parker Washington, an expected bounce-back from Brian Thomas Jr., and the return of Travis Hunter. This offense has the chance to be special, and Meyers could very well still deliver some value, but when Thomas and Washington were healthy from Weeks 13-18 last year, Meyers was the WR30.

players.name: Patrick Mahomes
players.take: Mahomes is coming off what was statistically the worst season of his career, which also culminated in a torn ACL. Even worse for fantasy managers: His fantasy production last season was redeemed by his rushing; he put up career highs in yards (422) and touchdowns (five). Mahomes looks to be healthy and ready to play in Week 1 but has already hinted that he will run the ball less.

players.name: Matthew Stafford
players.take: Stafford was the QB3 last year as the league's MVP. He returns virtually all of his offensive playmakers, so a high-end outcome is once again in-play for the 18th-year veteran. But simple regression to the mean coluld make him more of a borderline QB1 or QB2.

players.name: George Kittle
players.take: While Kittle tore his Achilles tendon in January, the 49ers reportedly have a “high level of confidence” that he’ll be ready to play by Week 1. We’re not putting it past Kittle to shatter the expected timeline for recovery on that type of injury, but it’s also probably best to keep expectations reasonable. If you take Kittle, have a plan to get another TE in your draft or to stream one until he’s a full go.

players.name: Kyle Monangai
players.take: Last season, Monangai, an unheralded seventh-round rookie, popped as the Kirkland-brand David Montgomery for Bears head coach Ben Johnson. He has low upside unless something happens to D’Andre Swift, but he’s talented and should get some snaps every week.

players.name: Khalil Shakir
players.take: The perfect example of a player more valuable in real life than in fantasy, Shakir led the Bills in targets, catches, and receiving yards last season but was not a top-40 fantasy receiver. Shakir is a willing blocker and clutch third-down pass catcher, but he does not have the volume or big-play ability to be a fantasy starter, especially after the Bills traded for DJ Moore.

players.name: Matthew Golden
players.take: Golden had little impact in his first regular season but shined against Chicago in the playoffs and now will replace Romeo Doubs in the starting lineup. Golden has never commanded big target volume, and the role he is taking over in the Packers offense has never garnered big volume either. Golden is faster than Doubs, so perhaps he can create more big plays, but Golden’s role is likely more valuable IRL than in fantasy.

players.name: KC Concepcion
players.take: You won’t find another first-round rookie wideout this late in drafts. The Browns have one of the worst QB situations (if not the worst) in the league and a lot of young talent surrounding Concepcion (Denzel Boston, Harold Fannin Jr., Jerry Jeudy). Considering the cost, KC is one of the higher-upside late-round picks at the position.

players.name: Tyler Allgeier
players.take: Always the bridesmaid, never the bride. Allgeier left Atlanta and signed in Arizona to get out from under the shadow of superstar running back Bijan Robinson … only to once again find himself quickly overshadowed, this time by Cardinals rookie Jeremiyah Love. Allgeier is sure to get some carries in the Cardinals backfield, but he’s only a handcuff option.

players.name: Isaiah Likely
players.take: An effortless pass catcher who could be the NFL’s best red zone target if the field were 6 inches wider, Likely followed John Harbaugh to the Giants in free agency. While Likely has been behind Mark Andrews in Baltimore for years, he now finds himself in a weak receiving corps in New York and has a serious chance to lead the team in receiving yards any week Malik Nabers is out.

players.name: Dalton Kincaid
players.take: Kincaid led all tight ends in yards per route run last season, but injuries (PCL, hamstring) and his questionable blocking ability kept him off the field at times, and he managed just 39 catches for 571 yards. If he’s healthy, he could be quite productive.

players.name: Keaton Mitchell
players.take: Mitchell has never had more than 400 rushing yards in a season, so we have to keep our expectations in check. With that said, Chargers OC Mike McDaniel has emphasized Mitchell’s pass game and his willingness to ride the hot hand in the backfield. Remember, McDaniel has produced fantasy explosions for multiple backs in one season. In 2023, Raheem Mostert and De'Von Achane were both top-five fantasy running backs under McDaniel.

players.name: Malik Willis
players.take: Willis went from Green Bay backup to Miami starting QB this offseason despite tallying just six starts in four years. Willis’s rushing upside is massive in theory, but in reality, he’s never run for 75 yards in a game, and betting markets project the Dolphins as the worst team in the NFL this season. Betting on Willis is betting on huge garbage-time stats.

players.name: Romeo Doubs
players.take: Doubs is an underrated player who will start for the Patriots after signing in free agency, but he’ll likely be opening up room for A.J. Brown more than he’ll be commanding a huge target volume. Doubs is more valuable to a real NFL team than a fantasy one.

players.name: Baker Mayfield
players.take: Mayfield struggled through a season from hell in 2025, battling through something like eight separate injuries on his way to disappointing real football (8-9, missed playoffs) and fantasy (QB18 in points per game) finishes. Now healthy, the veteran quarterback looks poised for a bounce-back year. Mayfield, who finished as the QB4 and tossed  41 touchdowns in 2024, should benefit from a healthier offensive line and a new offensive play caller in Zac Robinson—giving him a strong chance to provide value as a later-round QB pick.

players.name: Aaron Jones Sr.
players.take: Jones turns 32 in December and is coming off his worst season since his rookie year by basically any stat you’d want to pick. Jones has lost most short-down and distance work to Jordan Mason and is beginning to cede some passing work to Zavier Scott. He accepted a pay cut (of $4 million) to stay on the team, which rarely leads to a larger role.

players.name: Jalen Coker
players.take: The Panthers’ passing game will likely run through star receiver Tetairoa McMillan, but Coker has a chance to be a surprisingly high-volume complement. The third-year pro has flashed when given the opportunity, and now, with rookie Chris Brazzell out for the year and Xavier Legette still struggling to separate and stand out, he faces little competition for the no. 2 role.

players.name: Chris Rodriguez Jr.
players.take: Rodriguez joined the Jags on a two-year deal worth up to $10 million after three years in Washington. He rejoins Liam Coen (his college coach) in what projects to be a two-headed Jacksonville backfield, with Rodriguez working alongside Bhayshul Tuten. Coen has a history of turning overlooked backs into legitimate fantasy contributors, making Rodriguez an intriguing option later in drafts.

players.name: Jonah Coleman
players.take: Coleman is a fourth-round draft pick who joins J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey in a crowded Denver running back room. With Dobbins’s health struggles, Coleman has a real opportunity to make a splash this season as the early-down back in one of the league's most prolific offenses.

players.name: Xavier Worthy
players.take: Worthy dislocated his shoulder in Week 1 last year and struggled the rest of the season. Now that he’s healthy, the Chiefs will look to better utilize Worthy in the screen game and on crossers in an offense that desperately needs explosive plays.

players.name: Jared Goff
players.take: Goff is best utilized as a stable backup to a high-upside rushing QB. Goff is one of the few quarterbacks left who truly gives nothing from a rushing perspective, so virtually all of his fantasy points come from passing. Yet Goff has finished as a top-10 fantasy quarterback for three straight years in total points, partially because he’s durable and the Lions offense is awesome. But there is concern that the Lions’ typically elite offensive line might be merely average (or worse) this year, especially with center Cade Mays out for eight to 10 weeks.

players.name: Tyler Shough
players.take: Shough impressed as a second-round rookie last year, starting the final nine games of the season for the Saints while finishing as the QB12 in that stretch (17.1 points per game). With a full offseason of work as the established starter—plus the addition of a playmaking rookie pass catcher in Jordyn Tyson—Shough has a chance to really break out in 2026 and outplay his ADP.

players.name: Jordan Love
players.take: Love is a high-floor, low-ceiling pocket-passing QB. He’s had just one rushing TD in the past two seasons, so his fantasy upside is capped.

players.name: Dallas Goedert
players.take: Goedert exploded for 11 touchdowns last season, almost as many as he earned in his previous four years combined. With A.J. Brown gone, there’s more room in the offense, and Goedert is back on a $7 million deal.

players.name: Jordyn Tyson
players.take: Tyson might have a higher ceiling than any other rookie pass catcher this year. Opposite star receiver Chris Olave, he should get plenty of opportunities in head coach and play caller Kellen Moore’s high-tempo passing game, and he has the talent to produce big numbers early on in his career. The big hiccup for the rookie out of Arizona State, though, is concerns about his availability: Tyson missed games in all four of his college seasons and has already missed practices for the Saints this offseason due to lingering hamstring tightness.

players.name: Woody Marks
players.take: Marks saw action in 16 games as a rookie, racking up 703 yards and two rushing scores on 196 carries and adding 23 catches for 208 yards and three touchdowns through the air. He’ll play behind the newly signed David Montgomery, but he could make his impact felt in the pass game, spelling Montgomery on passing downs. Marks won’t likely have a ton of stand-alone value, but he’s a solid handcuff.

players.name: Juwan Johnson
players.take: Johnson quietly posted a 77-catch, 889-yard, three-touchdown line last year for the ascending Saints offense, finishing seventh among tight ends in targets (102). He’s not a flashy name, but Johnson should give fantasy drafters a late-round target who will actually get some volume in 2026. If he can up his touchdown total—which is possible with Taysom Hill now out of the equation—he could really surprise in fantasy this year.

players.name: Tyjae Spears
players.take: Spears projects as a receiving-down option in a low-scoring offense. The Titans have a new offensive play caller in Brian Daboll, so the pecking order and workload split could shift, but Spears is clearly behind Tony Pollard and should be drafted as a low-upside handcuff.

players.name: T.J. Hockenson
players.take: Hockenson was the no. 2 tight end in fantasy just a few years ago, but between a torn ACL and the J.J. McCarthy experience, it’s been a while since he was truly effective. Hockenson’s best days are likely behind him, but he is entering a contract year, so he could be a viable upside bet if the Vikings offense bounces back with Kyler Murray.

players.name: Makai Lemon
players.take: A first-rounder out of USC with fantastic hands, quickness, and effort as a blocker, Lemon does his best work over the middle but goes to an Eagles team that has not thrown much to that area of the field with Jalen Hurts at QB. Lemon has also missed much of minicamp and training camp with a hamstring injury, so he may not start right away.

players.name: Dylan Sampson
players.take: Sampson was a productive pass catcher and explosive playmaker last season, proving that he belongs on the field. He is the clear no. 2 behind Quinshon Judkins, who is making his way back from a broken leg. With that said, draft all Cleveland Browns at your own risk.

players.name: Sam Darnold
players.take: Darnold proved that his late-career breakout campaign with the Vikings in 2024 was no fluke, signing with the Seahawks last year and promptly leading them to a Super Bowl victory. Darnold’s fantasy numbers in Seattle dropped off from those 2024 Minnesota highs (when he was the QB9 in points per game) as he scraped out a QB23 finish. We’d expect something similar in the Seahawks offense again in 2026—which makes Darnold a floor play as a QB2 in super-flex leagues.

players.name: Tyrone Tracy Jr.
players.take: Tracy lost passing-down work and goal-line snaps to rookie Cam Skattebo last year, limiting his role to mostly between the 20s on early downs—ironic, considering Tracy is a converted college receiver. There will be plenty of work in this offense if Skattebo’s gnarly broken leg from last year hasn’t healed. But if Tracy is not playing on passing downs or at the goal line, his upside will be severely capped.

players.name: Alvin Kamara
players.take: Pretty much everyone, including the Saints, it seems, expected Kamara to retire, but the veteran back decided to show back up for work. That prompted a reworked one-year contract and some shuffling of expectations in the New Orleans backfield. Kamara is likely to have a role on passing downs; plus, he may see some carries deep in the red zone. But Travis Etienne will likely lead the way in New Orleans.

players.name: C.J. Stroud
players.take: Stroud threw for more than 4,000 yards and tossed 23 touchdowns and just five picks as a rookie, finishing as the QB8 in fantasy points per game. But he has struggled mightily to produce a repeat of that stellar start to his career. His numbers have dropped dramatically over the past two seasons, as has his value in fantasy, with QB28 (in 2024) and QB20 (last year) finishes in points per game. The Texans have made investments in the offensive line (first-rounder Keylan Rutledge, along with free agents Wyatt Teller and Braden Smith) and at receiver (adding Jayden Higgins and Jaylin Noel in last year’s draft) with the goal of stabilizing Stroud’s play, but the fourth-year quarterback really needs to make a jump in 2026.

players.name: Isiah Pacheco
players.take: The Lions signed Pacheco to a one-year deal in March after trading veteran RB David Montgomery to Houston. Pacheco is likely to be the change-of-pace back in Detroit behind Jahmyr Gibbs and could start if Gibbs gets hurt.

players.name: Brenton Strange
players.take: Strange is a good player who has popped here and there over the last few years. In fantasy football, tight ends most often break out when they are the first or second option in the passing game and have a path to heavy end zone usage. But Jacksonville is flush with pass catchers.

players.name: Bryce Young
players.take: For the most part, Young’s been a fantasy afterthought in his three years in the league, finishing no better than QB24 in any single campaign. He has a shot at making a jump in year four. But with both of his starting tackles likely to miss the beginning of the season with injuries, it seems unlikely that he’ll be anything other than a low-floor, low-ceiling option once again.

players.name: Oronde Gadsden II
players.take: The key to finding breakout tight ends is finding someone who can command volume on a high-scoring offense. The Chargers have Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston but no locked-in no. 3 option in the passing game, leaving a spot open for Gadsden, who put together a surprisingly productive rookie season with more than 600 receiving yards.
